Veel MKB’s reageren te traag omdat ze si: Many SMEs react too slowly because they do not consider external signals and internal priorities together. This leads to fragmented decisions: missing a grant, making an investment without a clear outcome, or assigning people to the wrong work.
Hoe je externe en interne veranderingen: Bringing external and internal change together (a practical framework) Use this simple, business-ready framework to turn an external signal into a concrete decision and measurable result: - Strategy: what is changing in our market or funding environment, and does it fit our long-term ambition? - Goals: which short- and medium-term goals will this affect (growth, margin, continuity)? - Finances: which additional financing or grant options are available, when do they apply, and what co-funding is needed? - Processes: which existing processes must be adapted or accelerated to meet grant conditions and market demand? - People: which roles or skills, internal or external, are needed to turn this opportunity into results? - Risks: which operational, legal or market-related risks emerge, and how can we mitigate them?
Sluit de verbeterlus: signaal → context: Close the improvement loop: signal → context → consequence → decision → action → result → learning Always follow the same closed loop. Here is a structure you can apply immediately, without technical jargon: 1) Signal (external): Bouwend Nederland reports a grant scheme for transforming existing buildings (source: bouwendnederland.nl). 2) Context (specific to your business): assess which current or planned projects, or which of your capabilities, directly match the scheme (for example, projects with potential for reconfiguration, adding floors or subdivision). 3) Consequence (scenarios): map out two scenarios: a) if we apply for the grant, what additional resources and timing are required; b) if we do not apply, what is the risk of lost revenue or competitive disadvantage? 4) Decision (concrete): decide whether to carry out a brief feasibility and grant eligibility check within 8 weeks for 1-2 promising projects. - Owner: operations director / innovation project manager. 5) Action (time-bound and verifiable): carry out a rapid grant assessment (maximum 4 weeks), including project selection, cost estimates, required process changes and staffing needs. Prepare an associated action plan with budget and named owners. - Action owner: innovation project manager. 6) Result (measure): within 6 weeks, a documented decision is available: the grant application has been submitted, or a deliberate decision has been made not to apply. - Measurable evidence: application submitted before the deadline (yes/no), and a baseline of lead time and estimated additional costs per project (in EUR and days) recorded. 7) Learning: after the grant process or pilot, compare the baseline with actual outcomes (lead time, direct costs) and update your standard processes and prioritization rules.
Wat meetbaar maken betekent (praktische: What making results measurable means (practical choices) - Metrics you can use immediately: whether a grant application exists (submitted / not submitted), the number of selected projects, baseline lead time (days) before action and measured lead time after the pilot, plus actual expenditure (EUR) versus the budget estimate. - Use simple dashboards or a shared spreadsheet: complicated tools are not necessary; what matters is that the owner, deadline and metric are clear.
Rol van Powerhouse (de motor, niet het p: The role of Powerhouse (the engine, not the product) Powerhouse can serve as a mechanism for collecting signals, placing them in context and making priorities visible — think of an internal engine that processes signals, supports verification steps and gives an overview of decisions, owners and measures. Importantly, final decisions remain human and controlled; systems only support and automate repetitive steps with explicit approval.
